title: CORS Preflight Requests and the OPTIONS Method
description: Understand why browsers send preflight OPTIONS requests and how ASP.NET Core responds to them.

data.text: Before sending certain cross-origin requests, the browser sends a preflight request. It uses the HTTP OPTIONS method to ask the server: "May I send the actual request with these headers and this method?" The server must respond with the right CORS headers, and only then does the browser send the real request.

terms.definition: An automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends to check whether the actual request is safe to send.
The real request (GET, POST, etc.) the browser sends after the preflight succeeds.
A cross-origin request that does not trigger a preflight because it uses only safe methods and standard headers.
A preflight header that tells the server which HTTP method the actual request will use.

data.title: When Does Preflight Happen?
data.text: A preflight is triggered when the request uses a method other than GET, HEAD, or POST, or when it sends non-simple headers such as Authorization, Content-Type: application/json, or custom headers.

data.caption: The preflight handshake before a cross-origin POST
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser as Browser
    participant Server as API Server
    Browser->>Server: OPTIONS /api/orders
    Note right of Browser: Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
    Note right of Browser: Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, authorization
    Server-->>Browser: 204 No Content
    Note left of Server: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
    Note left of Server: Access-Control-Allow-Methods: POST, GET
    Note left of Server: Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type, authorization
    Browser->>Server: POST /api/orders (real request)
    Server-->>Browser: 201 Created

data.text: When you call UseCors, ASP.NET Core automatically intercepts OPTIONS requests and returns the correct CORS headers. You usually do not need to write a controller action for OPTIONS unless you have very custom requirements.

data.title: Program.cs — CORS Middleware Handles OPTIONS Automatically
data.content: Enable CORS with a named policy and let the middleware respond to preflight requests.

data.text: With this setup, any OPTIONS request to a mapped controller endpoint receives a 204 response with the CORS headers. The browser then proceeds with the actual POST, PUT, DELETE, or other request.

The browser caches the preflight result so it does not ask the server for every single request. The Access-Control-Max-Age header controls how long the result is cached. ASP.NET Core sets a default, but you can tune it with SetPreflightMaxAge.

data.title: Program.cs — Setting Preflight Max Age
data.content: Cache preflight results for 10 minutes (600 seconds).

data.title: Expose Custom Headers
data.text: Use WithExposedHeaders when your API returns custom headers such as X-Total-Count or X-Request-Id. Without it, JavaScript cannot read those headers from a cross-origin response.

rows: Only simple headers (Accept, Accept-Language, Content-Language, Content-Type with simple values)
Sends OPTIONS first, waits for success, then sends actual request

data.title: Inspect a Preflight Request
data.description: Use browser DevTools to observe the preflight handshake.
steps: Open an ASP.NET Core API with CORS enabled.
From a different origin, use fetch() to POST JSON data with an Authorization header.
Open the Network tab in DevTools and filter by 'Fetch/XHR'.
Find the OPTIONS request before the POST request.
Inspect the request and response headers of the OPTIONS call.
data.expectedOutcome: You should see the browser send an OPTIONS request and the server respond with Access-Control-Allow-Origin and related headers before the POST is sent.

items.question: Do I need to create a controller action for OPTIONS?
items.answer: No. The CORS middleware handles OPTIONS automatically when UseCors is configured.

items.question: Why does my POST request fail with a CORS error even though I allowed the origin?
items.answer: The preflight may be failing. Check that Access-Control-Allow-Headers includes the headers your actual request uses (for example, Content-Type: application/json or Authorization).

items.question: Can I disable preflight completely?
items.answer: You cannot disable it in the browser, but you can avoid triggering it by sticking to simple requests: GET, HEAD, or POST with a simple Content-Type and no custom headers.

items.text: I can explain why browsers send a preflight OPTIONS request
I know the difference between a simple request and a preflighted request
I understand that ASP.NET Core handles OPTIONS automatically through the CORS middleware
I can use SetPreflightMaxAge and WithExposedHeaders to tune preflight behavior

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Preflight is an OPTIONS request that checks if the actual request is allowed
Non-simple methods, non-simple Content-Type, and custom headers trigger preflight
ASP.NET Core CORS middleware responds to OPTIONS automatically
SetPreflightMaxAge reduces the number of preflight requests the browser sends
data.takeaway: Next, you will learn best practices for CORS and how to troubleshoot common issues.
